rationale: Best configuration reaches 65.3% accuracy (macro-F1 0.559), matching the best zero-shot LLM reported in the source benchmark paper (Gemini 2.5 Flash 65.3%, literature comparator), but only with detailed label definitions (simple prompt 49.4%) and misinformation-class F1 0.08-0.20 (Sec. 3.1-3.2).

Inside the regex-flagged stratum weighted sensitivity 0.999 [0.997, 1.000] and specificity 1.000 (resting on 27 adjudicated negatives), but among 499,306 unflagged narratives only 14 of 42 adjudicated model positives were confirmed misses and stage/transport attributes have no reference standard (Table 3; §4.1; §5).

Jev accuracy 0.732 (D1) / 0.913 (CLINC-150) / macro-F1 55.0 (D3) vs Qwen3.6-27B likelihood 0.733/0.912/52.3 and Qwen3-14B verbal 0.680/0.728/52.7, but below trained BERT 0.940 and BGE-LR 0.948 on CLINC (-3.5 points; significant) and BGE 59.4 on D3 (Table 5; §5.1).

Zero-shot accuracy 9.80% (below the 22.79% majority constant) and 28.42% with 40 examples vs Random Forest 69.95% and Extra Trees 66.80%, which win in all 26 weeks; on a paired 100-record subset Jev-40 29% vs GPT-5.6 Sol 37% (McNemar p=0.2005) (Tables 1-2; §4.1-4.2).

Binary prompt-injection screening by frozen open readouts reaches mean accuracy 0.720 raw and 0.762 with rotations and label prior; rotations help on only 3 of 7 non-tied models (p=0.77) and 3 of 11 models fail the answer-mass gate (Table 1; §3).

Jev F1 0.856 at k=1 (precision 0.953, recall 0.778) vs Gemini 3.6 Flash 0.880, which wins discordant decisions at every k (p<0.001), while Jev wins on novel attacks at k=1 (74 vs 44, p=0.007) and k=2 and far exceeds Random Forest precision 0.598 (Tables 2-3; body figures used, abstract inconsistent).

On SemBench JEVDB-Flash quality is best or tied on 14/21 queries vs LOTUS/Palimpzest/ThalamusDB (Gemini 2.5 Flash) with deficits on 3, but on Shelob fixed-threshold mean F1 is 63.2-66.3% ranging from 23.8-30.4% (Q4) to 85.3-88.9% (Q1) (Tables 3-4; §4.2-4.3).

In-distribution macro-F1 0.620-0.644 (mean 0.63) vs rule tree R1 0.557-0.606 (n.s.) and supervised R2 0.887-0.934, and only after a label-free prior correction (0.41 without); beats leave-one-subtype-out R2 by +0.36 to +0.42 (p<1e-4) but 4 of 14 Holm comparisons are significant and all favour an LLM (§3.1-3.4; §3.6).

excluded_reason: no typed model measured or built (harness paper)
rationale: No typed decision model is measured; the paper defines five harness assurance properties and finds a real P4 scope-enforcement gap in the author's own NeuroSploit harness, i.e. evidence that scope enforcement belongs to harness code, not to model judgement (abstract; Sec. IX).

JevLite (open Qwen3-4B LoRA typed readout, 3-seed ensemble) reached AUROC .974 on 577 held-out turn decisions, non-inferior to the MiniMax-M3 LLM judge at the pre-registered .02 margin (+.027 [-.011, .065]) and not significantly better than a ModernBERT encoder, with ECE .052 vs .054, 100% vs 82.3% on legitimate calls, and a gray/legit deficit (38.1% vs 50.0%, n=3 scenarios) the authors place within seed noise; recipe was selected with test-set exposure and callers are synthetic (Sec. 5, Table 2, Table 3).

On 15 preregistered CSS annotation tasks (7,977 items) Jev trails the per-task best LLM on 14 of 15 with a median deficit of 11.6 macro-F1 points, significant after FDR correction on 12; the 0.6B open RLCD model is far lower (median macro-F1 0.361 vs 0.581) (Sec. 4.1, Table 1).

One-question Jev evaluator reaches Kendall tau 0.573 (RadEvalX) and 0.398 (RadEvalExpert) with expert error counts, beating an open NLI judge, and detects false negation with AUROC 0.977, but the local LLM-based RadMatch agrees better on clinically significant errors in both expert datasets (abstract; Sec. 5.1-5.3).

On 123 ContractNLI test contracts (2,091 judgments) Jev had 77.38% [75.99, 78.81] accuracy, below all seven hosted LLMs (78.96-83.21%; paired gap significant vs Gemini Flash-Lite +5.16 pp [3.49, 6.98] but not vs GPT-5.6 Luna [-0.05, 3.11]), at the lowest cost ($0.000228/contract) and median latency (1.24 s) (Table 1, Sec. 4.1).

Exploratory single runs with and without a Jev decision layer against one 13-vulnerability target: the Jev run hit 9/13 seeded scenarios vs 10/13 for the LLM-only run, reported 18 vs 16 findings, recalibrated 9 severities and finished 5 min 19 s faster, but the author states the runs lack statistical power and the severity comparison comes from a re-test with a changed harness (Sec. IX, Tables VI-VIII).

A generic zero-shot question reached median AUROC 0.886 [0.821, 0.952] over 31 alignment-failure benchmarks, beating TF-IDF/length baselines on 25 of 31 and matching the GPT-4o-mini scorer against human labels (kappa 0.809 vs 0.811); but the recommended use needs a threshold fitted on ten labels (median F1 0.706 at 0.5 vs 0.822 cross-validated, gain mostly on unvalidated labels) and parity fails per generator (GPT-3.5 kappa 0.668 vs 0.790) (Sec. 4.1, 4.4, 4.5).

Across 9 panels from 7 human-labelled benchmarks, Jev's accuracy differs significantly from flash-tier LLM judges in at most 8 of 27 paired comparisons, ahead mostly on binary checklist criteria and behind only on ordinal ones, at 16-325x lower cost (abstract; Sec. 4.1-4.2; Table 3).

Jev is the best typed model on R-Judge (AUROC 0.961 vs Laya 0.533) and AgentHarm and comparable to GPT-4.1, but all five reasoning judges have higher R-Judge Macro-F1 and Jev misses all 130 no-EI implicit injections on WAInjectBench (Sec. 4.2, 5.2; Tables 6-8).

Fine-tuned Laya-322M reaches 98.85% accuracy and 0.42% FPR on the 607-item clean Chinese DUCS-Bench split, but untuned Laya has 35.71% FPR and fine-tuning lowers SafetyBench-ZH accuracy 60.33%->56.81% unless 458-item replay is mixed in (65.05%) (Table II; Table V; Sec. IV-F).

On 5,219 agent trajectories Jev's benchmark-averaged positive-class F1 is 77.8 vs 74.1 for the best generative judge GLM-5.2 (paired difference 2.7 points, exploratory bootstrap 95% CI 0.5-4.8) at a common threshold, though GLM leads on 2 of 4 benchmarks and is more precise (91.9 vs 77.1) (abstract; Table 2; App. B). [Recoded in review: wins on 2 of 4 benchmarks with lower precision; mixed across tasks is Q under v3]

On a 50-way CWE classification of 1,916 CyberSecEval snippets Jev beat all six open-weight LLMs but had lower top-1 than GPT-5.6-Sol (0.458 vs 0.495) with higher top-3/top-5 and similar MRR; diagnosis-guided repair raised the security pass rate 0.635 to 0.707 (LLM-guided 0.661) but broke 89 secure samples (LLM-guided 79) (Abstract, Sec. IV).

Re-running 5 of 44 Just Ask Jev legs (1,155 items) reproduced AUROC (median absolute difference 0.0036; TensorTrust-hijack 0.9476), but F1 at threshold 0.5 was low (0.158 on TensorTrust-hijack, recall 8.8%) vs 0.947 with a threshold fitted on labels; median F1 gain +0.254 and none of five fitted thresholds was 0.5 (README tables).

With structural receiving checks, the Jev semantic gate withheld all 12 unsupported releases on 48 synthetic episodes, but on 120 VitaminC pairs it accepted 1 of 120 benchmark-negatives (confidence 1.00) and withheld 38 of 120 positives (label agreement 194/240, 80.8%), so autonomous reliability is not established (ADDENDUM.md; rr-jev-vitamin-c/RESULTS.md).

On 30 public Argentine Supreme Court metadata records Jev classified legal area correctly in 60% (Kev 20%) versus 96.7% for deterministic rules, and procedural vehicle in 96.7% versus rules 100% (Resultados table).

As a candidate checker Jev was 5-60 points more accurate than GPT-5.6 Luna without reasoning (e.g. sparse ordering 98.3% vs 85.0%) and matched reasoning-enabled Luna on two moderate logic sets at about one-fifth to one-sixth of the cost, but fell below it on sparse ordering (98.3% vs 100%) and the hardest set (4/5 vs 5/5) (Tables 2-3, Sec. 6.4).

On identical 500-600-item samples of seven public moderation, hallucination, NLI and injection tasks, Jev had the highest AUROC of the cheap-tier LLMs on all six binary tasks (0.90-0.99), tied Claude Haiku 4.5 on ANLI, and was never significantly worse than a cheap-tier model, though frontier Claude Sonnet 4.6 (42-97x the cost) beat it on ANLI-R3 and HaluEval-Dialogue; full-split re-runs (54,634 decisions) stayed within the sample CIs (Tables 2-3, Table 12, Sec. 6).

The open Laya judge (laya 0.3.4) is near-perfect when the answer is explicit (0.9909, n=220) but collapses on absent evidence (no_support 0.3091, n=220) where the generative LLM scores 1.00, reaches 0.4583 vs 1.00 on authority location and 0.225 vs 0.75-0.90 on 77-class intent, and its errors do not complement the LLM's (judge-only correct 0-2 vs LLM-only 23-27) (abstract; Sec. 6.1, 7).

On 270 policy-derived authorization cases x 3 repetitions, Jev's permission Brier was lower than GPT-4.1 mini's (0.0263 vs 0.0555; difference -0.0292 [-0.0557, -0.0070]) with 6 vs 13 tier-only false allows, but not distinguishable from DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (0.0267 vs 0.0337, interval includes zero), and Jev denied 18/357 reference-hold attempts vs 1-2 for the comparators; labels come from an author-written oracle without human adjudication (Tables III-IV, Sec. V).

Jev 1.13.0 decided 272/300 cases correctly (90.67% [86.8, 93.5]) and the open KEV-4B 273/300, both above the generative GLM 5.3 FlashX (260/300; Jev minus GLM +4.00 pp [0.33, 7.34], GLM losing 33 truncated outputs), while the open CLM v0.1-8B scored 111/300 by returning hold throughout (RESULTS-SUMMARY tables).

Related but non-supporting paragraphs cut HotpotQA accuracy 0.84 to 0.75 while confidence stays at 0.83, and an uninformative cue raises the guessed option by 0.65; an added note that context may be irrelevant restores 0.84 (§4.1-4.3).

On misleading matrix games accuracy is 28-37% with the lure chosen 53-71%, ALFWorld misleading steps 36% (seen) / 43% (unseen) vs 93-99% on aligned steps, and 90% / 89% of errors go to the lure vs 50% / 12% by chance (§4.1; §5.1; §8).

Mean cyberattack recall 0.34 vs 0.60-0.71 for other classes (R2 0.87), and on the look-alike family set the agreement gate accepted 21 of 76 windows that were attacks (accept precision 0.579 [0.467, 0.683]) (§3.5-3.6).

On 510 reconstructed InjecAgent cases the original injection selected the attacker target in 9/510 (1.8%) and the enhanced attack in 0%; 24 queries of score-feedback optimisation raised validated ASR only to 3.5% [0.0, 10.0] (18 cases) with confident-hijack rate 0.2%, although attacker probability rose (+0.043 to 0.084) and successes clustered on small-margin cases (Sec. 5.1-5.5, Table 2).

A probability-guided search (<=64 accepted queries) for fluent context additions redirected Jev on 312 of 508 initially correct decisions (61.4%, Wilson 57.1-65.5), 229 ending with >=0.7 on the wrong option; a plain Qwen scorer flipped 64.9% and open typed models (OpenSourceJev, Von) up to 73.2% of their own correct items (Abstract, Sec. 4.2, Table 1).

On 812 typed questions (9,744 single-edit variants), one unverified observer opinion appended to the state flipped 12.1% [8.5, 15.5] of decisions (+11.1 pp over re-run noise), statistically tied with the strongest injected command (10.1%), at least one of nine delivered attacks flipped 29.2% of questions, and 88.8% of multi-option targeted flips landed on the attacker's option (Table 2, Sec. 4.2-4.3).
Jev misses all 130 WAInjectBench injections without explicit instructions, assigning unsafe probability <0.1, with 130 false negatives at confidence >=0.95 (Sec. 4.2, 5.2).

Against one due-diligence application, all nine attacker x difficulty combinations broke Jev at least once and the strongest of three adaptive attackers succeeded in 25 of 27 runs (about turn 4, about $0.50 per break); marking content untrusted made no difference (16/27 vs 16/27); Jev 59% overall vs 67-100% for non-reasoning comparators and 19-70% with reasoning enabled (blog tables).

Against Kev-0.8B the strongest of 15 attacks flipped 5/45 action-gate (11%, 95% CI 2-24%) and 12/45 investment decisions (27%, 11-44%); confidence fell for almost any added text, so the model did not recognise attacks (Sec. 5.2-5.4).

On the open Kev-0.8B with four questions per call, the strongest planted note per item made at least one related answer wrong in 89% (77/87) of eligible action-gate items and two or more in 29%, and when it flipped allow/block the risk answer was also wrong 48.4% vs 8.4% (H1 supported in 3 of 4 pairs); all results are for Kev-0.8B, not Jev (Sec. 5.2, Sec. 6.2).

Swapping yes/no names against fixed rubrics flips 50.5 Jev answers per 100 (CI 46.2-54.7; retest floor 1.3) with AUC 0.89 to 0.31 and 97.2 on derailment; Laya 91.3 and larger open decoders 4.2-6.5; neutral digits/random strings keep Jev within 2.8 flips (§5.2; Fig. 3).

Reversing option order changes the answer on 32.8% (banking20) and 33.4% (newsgroups) of items over 11 models; added rotation averaging lowers this to 0.138/0.183 (injection 0.180 to 0.000) but does not remove it (§3; Table 1; §7.1). [Recoded in review: order reversal flips 32.8-33.4%; rotation averaging is an added mitigation, so rule (iv) gives N]

With uninformative evidence ties follow the order chances are mentioned (99.6%) and Choice puts 0.98 on a 40% outcome, while 14 rewordings preserve ranking (AUROC 0.87-1.00) but shift absolute levels so thresholds must be set per wording (App. C; Table 4; §4.2).

Preregistered hypothesis that calibration degrades on Indian English dialect text was rejected in the opposite direction: Jev's dialect ECE 0.063 was the lowest of 22 models (next 0.181) and its F1 the only positive point estimate vs the best LLM (+4.2, CI -3.9 to +11.5); a single dialect task, which the authors say cannot certify fairness (Sec. 4.3).

Swapping yes/no option names over fixed definitions flips 76.9% of Laya decisions vs 6.5% for 0/1 names (+70.4 pp, 95% CI 67.6-73.1) and inverts AUC 93.8%->23.2%; hosted Jev flips 32.5% (AUC 81.5%->58.1%, test-retest <=1.33%) and Open-Jev 19.5%, with 0% type errors throughout (Sec. 4.1, 4.5; Tables 1, 6).

Author-built 9B 'System One' scorer (SubJudge, digit-token readout) achieves the lowest individual MAE on PluriHarms (0.1659 vs 0.168 Kimi-K3) and beats frontier LLMs on iNews arousal/dominance, but no group-fairness or wording/order stability test is reported and Jev is not tested (Sec. 3.1; Tables 1-2).

On runtime-declared templates that change only the question, fine-tuned open Laya returned its trained answer for 0.982-0.995 of item-seed pairs (0.801 act-and-wrong), whereas hosted Jev read the new questions (>=0.98 accuracy on 6 of 8 templates; 0.677 on renamed keys) (Sec. VI-C, Table V).

Jev's source-attribution x argument interactions were small (US CODEPINK-College Republicans -0.0197; five European pairs |I|<=0.0314, all below the adopted 0.05 reference) vs -0.154 to -0.449 for chat models; the author cautions that Jev used a different rubric with mid-scale scores (1.80-2.43 of 4) and that this does not establish debiasing (Sec. 4, 4.4, App. B).

Across ten SemEval corpora in six languages, frozen Jev plus 488 CPU-fitted coefficients gave the lowest aggregate Task-1 RMSE (1.0645, an untested 0.0018 below the next team), but raw scores reached only 2.0731, it trailed the best published score on 8 of 10 corpora, and extraction beat fine-tuned Llama-3.3-70B and GPT-OSS-120B baselines but trailed a generative retrieval-and-rules system by about 4 points and was weakest on Chinese laptop (Sec. 4.2-4.4, Tables 2-4).

PACT training on an open single-token typed model lowers answer flips under answer-code relabelling to 9.8% vs 13.8% for the published Nimble recipe and 23.5% for the base model on a frozen 324-item holdout over three seeds, reducing but not removing the bias (abstract; results table, Sec. VI). [Recoded in review: base model flips 23.5% under relabelling; only the authors' added training lowers it, so rule (iv) gives N]

Over 288,000 VSM-2013 answers, Jev without a persona answered like its own American personas (0.08 on an American-to-Saudi scale in English, 0.06 in Arabic), reproduced 87% of the human Saudi-US difference in English but 62% in Arabic with long-term orientation reversed, and shifted profiles in stereotyped ways by age and gender, in all eight request designs (Abstract, Fig. 1, Sec. 4.7).

On the authors' own CJ-Bench, the open Chinese-Jev (initialised from Laya Multilingual) reached 69.20% vs hosted Jev 68.35% on general Chinese decisions and 87.65% vs 84.29% on medical, but trailed Jev on legal (60.10 vs 68.35) and finance (64.72 vs 78.39), 92% of Jev's average; both typed models far exceeded the generative Qwen3.5-2B baseline (32.95% general) (Tables 1-2, Sec. 4.2).

Rotating answer options left accuracy unchanged (MMLU calculation subjects 94.3%), but accuracy fell from 97.2% in English to 37.4% for Nigerian Fulfulde on Belebele and to 33.8-70.3% for 16 African languages on AfriXNLI (English 90.5%); both open LLM references degrade likewise (Sec. 4.5-4.6, Table 6).

Jev put 38.8% of ANLI predictions and 51.3% of its errors on Neutral despite balanced labels; across 36 ordinal datasets decisions used only 67-76% of gold effective support (nominal 87-102%), two random option orders agreed on 74.4% of ordinal items, and finer scales cut utilisation to 26-75% at K=14 (Abstract, Sec. 4.1-4.3).

Hosted Jev flipped 2.9%/1.9% of decisions under option reordering (customer service/voice) and 1.7% between Simplified and Traditional script, whereas open Laya multilingual flipped 20.6%/10.8% and 12.8%, and a Qwen3.5-2B logit probe 2.9%/8.0% and 2.2% (README results table, current version beyond v0.2).

Jev rejects all 6,336 directed racial-superiority claims (mean P(true) about 3%), but when forced to name one group White receives 51.12% of first picks and wins 6 of 8 traits, with gender picks also stereotyped; option order was not counterbalanced, so a position effect is possible (Figs. 1-2, 5).
Argmax was stable across six option orders in 93.3% of cases for both Jev and Kev (n=30) (Resultados table).

With 2-3 equally eligible machines Jev gave dominant probability to the first one introduced in the context (NEXA 93%, ZEXA 86%, KELT 84%) and the preference followed context-order reversal (AORA 90%) while answer-option reversal barely moved it (92%); exploratory single runs on synthetic items (Sec. 4.10-4.15).

In an item-paired XNLI 2x2 the state-language effect on AUROC was +0.3150 [+0.2427, +0.3884] under Chinese criteria and +0.1660 under English for small open typed models (NanoJev, von), and Laya kept a language gap (English AUC 0.984 vs Chinese 0.568) (paper-zh Sec. 4.9, 4.13).
Renaming the no-action option to 'witness: observe without acting' (with a short preface) raised its probability by up to 0.28 in otherwise identical situations (Abstract, J2).

On 7,081 author-generated held-out Polish decisions hosted Jev scored 0.780 and English-oriented open typed models 0.59-0.78 (losing 13-23 points relative to English), while the Polish-trained open basal-1.0-4.5B reached 0.884; it tied Jev on 1,479 held-out English decisions (0.741 vs 0.736) but trailed it on public JevBench (0.740 vs 0.861), so closing the language gap required language-specific training (Table 23, Sec. 20).

Answers were stable across ten runs (spread <=0.08) but rewording the same dilemma moved them much more: trolley diversion 0.99 as a Choice vs 0.78 as a yes/no question, and opposite conclusions on meaning vs survival between framings (paper Sec. IV-F; README).

In 26,796 calls on Taiwan's sovereignty Jev's status index (0.40/0.26/0.40 in Traditional/Simplified Chinese/English) was below every generative model and it chose PRC formulations in Simplified Chinese forced choice regardless of option order, yet it never chose a label listing Taiwan under China (Claude Sonnet 5: 42% in Simplified Chinese); rankings depend on the instrument (Abstract, Sec. 4.2-4.6).

On 41 supplier-payment texts x 3 reruns (492 observations), open Laya was perfectly repeatable on identical inputs but meaning-preserving rewordings gave 32.38-56.67% pairwise decision disagreement, swapping Laya checkpoints changed 92.68%/78.05% of ternary decisions (36.59%/43.90% at the approve gate), and removing class definitions moved 19/41 typed-decisions outputs across the approve gate (Results).

Over 453 held-out CONFLICTS items in four prompt configurations, mean confidence on wrong answers stays flat at 0.56-0.58 (max 0.96-1.00, mean prob gap -0.48 to -0.50) and correct/wrong confidence separation is only 0.073-0.166; authors judge confidence too weak to gate automation (Sec. 3.3, Sec. 4).

Mean probability is conservative rather than calibrated within each decision group (Fig. 3a), the standalone transport question and gated post-crash condition disagree on 192 and 105 narratives (§4.3), and attribute calibration is unmeasured; aggregates rely on adjudication-based misclassification correction.

Shipped ECE 0.033 (D1) and 0.032 (CLINC) vs Qwen3-14B verbal 0.117/0.204 and Qwen3.6-27B likelihood 0.061/0.044, but 0.251 pooled on D3 needing per-task temperature scaling to reach 0.038; Kev-9B stored temperature degrades CLINC ECE 0.051 to 0.377 (Table 6).

Against a matched generative SFT baseline ECE falls 0.2589 to 0.0806 (classification), 0.2981 to 0.0114 (multi-label), 0.4204 to 0.0408 (counting), 0.1267 to 0.0913 (regression) in-distribution (Table 2); secondary probe: with the true candidate removed it picks a runner-up (0.88) instead of signalling absence (§5.4; App. B.3).

Label-free rotations plus prior move banking20 ECE only 0.251 to 0.223; a temperature fitted on labels reaches 0.088 but raises Granite-3.3-8B ECE 0.270 to 0.301 on JevBench, and the prior lowers BEV accuracy 68.01% to 65.01% (Table 1; §4.3; §7.2-7.3).

SmoothECE 0.015-0.033 on familiar closed-choice tasks (CLINC150, PopQA, MMLU-Redux, TriviaQA) but p_max 0.80 on a fair die and 0.52 for fabricated entities, and past the knowledge boundary log loss 0.71 is worse than 50/50 with 0.19-0.23 overconfidence left after recalibration (§4.1; Table 3).

Training-free Qwen3.5-4B readout reaches 81.4% on JevBench with ECE 0.057 (SemIf 0.061; Winnow-12B 0.058) but Qwen3-0.6B ECE is 0.278, and one epoch of intent fine-tuning drops JevBench to 76.2% with yes-bias and suppressed none-of-the-above while validation loss improves (Table 2; §4.3.2).

Against 2,416 blinded human labels raw Jev was miscalibrated (slope 1.63, Spiegelhalter test rejected, mean probability 4.8% vs weighted base rate 2.7%: under-extreme and level-shifted, not over-confident); of two frontier arms one was worse (slope 2.55) and one better (ECE 0.0027 vs 0.0231); out-of-fold Platt recalibration cut pooled ECE 0.0231 to 0.0069 (Sec. 4.2, 4.4, Table 9).

Median ECE 0.157 [0.108, 0.233] beat the verbalised confidence of 16 of 19 LLMs but not three frontier Claude models (0.066-0.075; intervals overlap); on empathy 78% of items had confidence >=0.9 at accuracy 0.383 (ECE 0.538), and the preregistered calibration hypothesis was unsupported (Sec. 4.2, 4.4).

Used zero-shot to estimate whether other LLMs' answers are correct, Jev reached AUROC 0.666 [0.638, 0.691] on 1,718 text responses (above verbalized-confidence baselines 0.610-0.649 and a GPT-5-mini judge 0.532, far below the trained PINOCCHIO 0.868) but ECE 0.133, worse than recalibrated baselines (0.009-0.034) and the LLM judge (0.110), and the authors conclude it gives no usable correctness signal off the shelf (Table 3; App. E.10).

Single-call error-detection AUROC 0.875/0.745/0.827 vs GPT-6 0.894/0.907/0.831 on RewardBench/JudgeBench/HaluEval; Brier 0.113/0.297/0.196 vs 0.115/0.095/0.213, with Jev's HaluEval advantage reversed on adjudicated labels; temperature scaling fitted on pilot data helped one task and hurt two (Sec. 7.2).

Raw sentence-level ECE is 0.1192 (holdout ECE 0.1235) versus 0.1045 for the open NLI baseline on 19,513 ReXErr examples, and becomes 0.0077 only after isotonic recalibration on a holdout (Sec. 5.6; App. G).

Probabilities calibrated when pooled (ECE 0.047) but not within benchmarks: median per-benchmark ECE 0.168 vs 0.074 expected under perfect calibration, 24 of 31 exceeding the null, from base-rate mismatch (median 0.125); confidence still supports selective use (top-half accuracy 0.793 to 0.933) (Sec. 4.4).

Jev's probabilities are calibrated on the binary panels, but its confidence ranks its own errors only weakly on ordinal panels (error-detection AUROC 0.57-0.70 on six, 0.49 on ELLIPSE) (Sec. 6; Table 3).

LAVOIR (open Laya-based ModernBERT encoder) is statistically indistinguishable from the Bayes ceiling on seen schemas and a Gini cap stops it asking when confident, but out-of-distribution calibration is weak (ABCD ECE 0.19), it is wrong on 19% of ABCD cases where its confidence is at least 0.99, and zero-shot schemas reach only 0.51-0.52 vs a 0.667 ceiling (Sec. 7.1-7.2, Limitations).

On 480 negation pairs Jev's P(X)+P(not X) misses 1 by 0.064 (95% CI 0.055-0.072) vs 0.293 for Qwen3.8-27B first-token and 0.122 verbalized, but Jev is still incoherent: violations about 5x its repeat-noise floor (0.013) and single-label probabilities summing to 1.14 (abstract; Sec. 5.1-5.2).

Independent preregistered study: the released Laya Typed-Decisions checkpoint was uniformly under-confident (signed gap -0.214); one disjointly fitted temperature cut held-out ECE from 0.204 to 0.037, but the frozen selection rule picked an overfitting isotonic calibrator and H2 failed on both tracks (Abstract, Sec. 4.2, Sec. 6).

Across 72,000 questions on TREC, CLINC150 and MASSIVE, directly asked category probabilities disagreed with summed fine-label probabilities by mean total variation 0.219-0.349 for Jev and 0.424-0.689 for Laya, which the author calls substantial incoherence (Abstract, Sec. 5, 9).

On MetaMedQA Jev was better calibrated than GPT-6 Sol (ECE 0.063 vs 0.146) but its confidence discriminated worse on DiagnosisArena (AUROC 0.645 vs 0.768); it chose 'I don't know' for 17/162 (10.5%) unanswerable items vs 8.6% for GPT-6 Sol, and was over-confident on every benchmark by 5.8-13.6 points (Sec. 3.3-3.4).

On 365 synthetic items with known P(A), Jev's Noul (mean OVL 0.918) and Score (0.886) probabilities tracked ground truth but binary Choice was distorted (0.764; open SemIf 0.629) and less invariant across renderings; an in-sample fitted uncertainty map raised median Choice OVL 0.771 to 0.903 (Table 1, Sec. 3-5, App. A).

Against a seed-matched cross-entropy-only control PACT lowers NLL by 26% and halves seed spread, with calibration relying on a fitted three-parameter contextual temperature; accuracy is not raised over the published recipe (84.6 vs 85.2%) (abstract; Sec. VI).

On 1,800 class-balanced accelerometer windows (5,400 decisions) Jev's probabilities were poorly calibrated: ECE 0.10-0.50 across nine dataset-representation cells (best representation 0.253, 0.349, 0.129) with mean maximum probability 0.37/0.58/0.30 against argmax accuracy 0.11/0.24/0.17, and 86 vectors failed validity; the generative Claude baseline returned no probabilities (Table 3, Sec. 4).

Jev's confidence was lower in Arabic and for Saudi personas and followed the language of the framing rather than of the items; the authors note this could flag answers resting on less evidence but cannot show calibration because value items have no correct answer (Sec. 4.6, Sec. 5.4).

Chinese-Jev General had ECE 3.78% vs hosted Jev 11.45% and Qwen3.5-2B 43.68% on general tasks, but after domain fine-tuning the specialists' average ECE (12.08%) exceeded Jev's (5.57%) and rose on legal (15.37% to 17.45%) (Tables 1-2, Sec. 4.2).

On 1,000 exact-posterior worlds Jev failed the operational coherence criterion (all nine relation pass-rate bounds <0.95) and had the largest calibration gap (0.1952) and canonical decision loss (0.1336 vs always-defer 0.10), yet smaller complement, coarsening and permutation residuals than Kev and the generative readouts (e.g. complement 0.0929 vs 0.1155-0.8000) (Sec. 6.1-6.3, Tables 2-3).

Choice probabilities well calibrated (pooled ECE 0.028 over 279,925 answers, unweighted mean 0.061; Qwen 0.063, Gemma 0.208), but multi-label Noul over-predicts yes (mean 0.209 vs observed 0.041) and binary probabilities need task thresholds (UNFAIR-ToS micro-F 0.499 to 0.748) (Sec. 4.3).

Decision-level compression on ordinal scales coexists with candidate probabilities that remain broad for most models, so graded probabilities partly preserve scale information that argmax decisions lose (Jev relative utilisation 95.9% at K=2 to 54.5% at K=14) (Sec. 4.3, Conclusion).

With Qwen3-1.7B over 3 seeds, two-stage RLCD matched GRPO+TS accuracy on GSM8K-Verify (92.2% vs 91.8%) with far better selective prediction (AURC 0.034 vs 0.061; 81.1% vs 19.4% of items decidable at 5% error), beat all reasoning baselines on MMLU-Pro (+5.3 points over SFT+TS), and on annotator-disagreement ChaosNLI matched rather than beat cross-entropy (JSD 0.075 vs 0.074) (Table 1, Table 3, Sec. 5).

Menu Choice with a None option gives 99% answer-present accuracy but 7% correct rejection on arithmetic (purchase totals 94% vs 24%; inventory 14/128), surviving relabelling and repositioning, while reasoning Qwen3.5-9B reaches 100% in both conditions (§4.2-4.5; Figs. 3 and 5).

After tuning a Jev prompt separately for each dataset, held-out ECE was 0.027 on 3,066 WiC pairs and 0.025 on 612 ChaosNLI stories with most bins within sampling error, but the author says the tuning step is critical (untuned scores bear no relation to ground truth) and top bins understate the true rate, making it less suited to high-confidence uses (Methodology, Results, Conclusion).

In a 13-run reproduction of Laya's RLCD fine-tune (three seeds for main arms), the RL term makes inference over-sharp (fitted binary temperature 1.16->1.72 and NLL 0.871->0.928 as noise rises 0.5->2) and CE-only matches or beats RL+CE on every proper score; calibration comes from distillation plus temperature scaling (report abstract; Sec. VI; Tables III, V).

Statistical argument (no new data) that calibration is a property of model and data distribution, so vendor calibration need not transfer to a user's production data; recommends treating Jev outputs as scores and recalibrating (e.g. Platt scaling on a few hundred labels).

Jev's shipped calibration held on Chinese voice routing (ECE 0.035, n=323; refit did not help) and scam detection (0.952, ECE 0.073, n=21), but open Laya's binary over-confidence exceeded its shipped correction range; the Qwen logit probe collapsed on binary judgments (scam ECE 0.39-0.42) (README key findings 2 and 5; results table).

Across 738,164 live Choice answers the returned confidence equals (p_max-1/N)/(1-1/N) within mean residual 0.005, so it rescales top probability and rises with padded options (formula-derived: 0.20 at N=2 to 0.58 at N=20 for p_max 0.60, not an observed manipulation); identical repeated calls moved confidence 0.84-0.88 and flipped labels on a flat question (7 vs 2 of 9) (Sec. 1; Table 2).
At confidence >=0.90 Jev's legal-area answer was correct in only 12 of 16 cases, with errors at confidence 0.99 and 1.00 (Resultados).

Single calls on 6 states: Noul probabilities put conflict (0.50-0.57) and ignorance (0.46-0.48) in one band, but a Choice schema naming both states separated the four conflict/ignorance cases with probability 1.0 (controls also correct), binary Choice showed a directional bias (0.67-0.85 toward red), and Score separated the extremes (2.04 vs 3.95); the author disclaims collapse per se (Tables 2-5; Sec. 7-8).
With no eligible option Jev put 83% on an ineligible machine, but when an explicit 'none satisfies' option was added it chose it, so abstention works only if the schema offers it (Sec. 4.6-4.7).

Jev's raw probabilities had the lowest mean Brier of all systems (0.103 vs 0.116-0.159 for five LLMs) and after cross-fitted Platt recalibration stayed better than the cheap tier and GPT-5.4 (0.076 vs 0.101-0.130) but not Claude Sonnet 4.6 (0.071); raw ECE 0.104 was similar to Haiku's 0.101 and one paraphrase raised BoolQ ECE to 0.30 (Table 8, Sec. 4, Sec. 7).
On 1,100 binary items Laya's ECE is 0.2259 vs 0.0028 for the LLM and its Brier 0.2571 is worse than a constant predictor's 0.2400, despite AUC 0.7136 (95% CI 0.682-0.745) (abstract; Sec. 6.2).

Laya multilingual's observed accuracy was below its mean confidence in every band (e.g. 0.90-0.95: 73% accuracy vs 92.9% confidence; >=0.95: 96.3% vs 99.2%), consistent with documented over-confidence of raw outputs (Sec. 3.5).

excluded_reason: deterministic rule engine; no typed model despite the name
rationale: Full text shows no typed decision model is measured: Bajev is a deterministic Kleene three-valued rule engine (threshold, keyword and hashing-embedding agents) that scored 100/100 with zero false certainty on an author-written corpus plus 105 unit tests, and 'JEV' appears only in its name; recorded empirical=no so it is excluded from typed-model tallies (Sec. 4-5, Sec. 10).

Eliciting bilateral truth tuples on ten constructed items, Jev (5 repeats) declared the liar sentence Order-0 like gpt-4o-mini and deepseek-chat but with the weakest margin (T+F 1.01-1.04), turned unambiguous facts into order 1 through noise in one probe, and like the LLMs did not reach designed intermediate orders; its outputs varied from call to call (Sec. 3.3, Sec. 4, Table 2).

Open small typed models gave uninformative confidence: NanoJev p_true lay entirely in 0.664-0.896 with none below 0.5 and von entirely below 0.474, with heavily overlapping positive/negative ranges (paper-zh Sec. 4.1, 5.2).

Preregistered (48,300 calls): confidence predicted own errors beyond page difficulty (AUROC +0.039 and +0.005, p=.0005) but tracked presentation (over-confident 0.10 on clean pages, under-confident 0.04 on reworked pages at matched accuracy, diff -0.136 [-0.173, -0.099]); with no evidence and no opt-out it answered at 0.82 confidence at chance; with an explicit no-action option it held 0.98 when nothing was left but its action threshold (0.39-0.44) ignored stakes (ideal 0.50-0.90) (Abstract, J1-J2).

Round-one answers based on a single word of biography sat as far from 0.5 as better-informed ones, although one extra fact moved answers by a median 0.15 (up to 0.67) and changed three of ten bunker places, so the model did not signal insufficient information (paper Sec. IV; README).

In a preregistered test on 1,500 ChaosNLI items, Jev's Choice ECE rose from 0.076 on the most-agreed quartile to 0.339 on the least-agreed (bias-corrected Delta 0.264 [0.244, 0.278]) with mean confidence 0.807 where 46.8% of annotators agreed; Noul degraded less (inconclusive), confidence still ranked contested items (AUROC 0.744), one temperature could not fix both strata, and Jev was far better calibrated than the local generative Qwen2.5-1.5B baseline (Abstract, Table 2, Sec. 7.5-7.8).

On the UAV benchmark with ground-truth epistemic uncertainty, open Laya-421M zero-shot reached accuracy 0.399 (majority 0.366), Brier 0.751 and confidence-vs-error AUROC 0.655, collapsing toward the prior while posting an ECE that looks acceptable; ECE varied 0.034-0.113 across option rotations (Abstract, Sec. 5 F6-F7, Conclusion).

Theory: Lemma 1 proves marginal calibration is not preserved under latent regime shift and every permutation-invariant audit statistic (ECE included) has zero power to detect it; checked only by simulation, 'nothing here is an empirical claim about' Jev (Abstract, Sec. 3, 7).

Answer-mass statistic exposed a template fault (gpt-oss m=0.000 with plausible-looking answers) and the stopping rule certifies agreement with full rotation at bound 0.0079 on 2 of 4 cells; the serving threshold was selected and certified on the same states (held-out disagreement 4/300) (§3; §5; Table 3; §9).

Conceptual: argues that qualification attrition means downstream evaluators cannot restore qualifications lost upstream, so auditability depends on preserving them up to the point of authorisation (§6.2; §8.3).

Writing a separately obtained prediction into the state raises game accuracy from 32-35% to 94% (the prediction itself is 90% correct), and given a written wrong action Jev best-responds to it in 24/26 calls, so intermediate facts become inspectable audit points (§4.3; Table 2).

With arithmetic in code and semantic relations asked as atomic Choices, Jev got 100/100 semantic and 50/50 downstream-exact answers, tied with five other configurations; the seven wrong intermediate selections that correct final labels concealed (581 of 588 outputs exact, all on one culture-history question) came from three comparator LLMs (Sec. 3.1-3.2, Table 1).

Model rankings by baseline accuracy and by correctness across 12 repeated request conditions diverge: Jev had the lowest hosted baseline accuracy (77.38% vs 78.96-83.21%) but kept 23/30 anchors correct in all 12 responses (second to Claude Sonnet 5's 24; difference one target), with 5 anchors repeated wrong throughout, so agreement alone does not establish correctness (Tables 1-2, Sec. 4.2-4.3).

Secondary evidence review of 28 papers (19-24 Sep 2026): the typed readout has not shown an independent accuracy advantage over comparable label-probability readouts, gains are mainly latency and cost, and only 1 of 27 papers passes the option-name test; a review, so excluded from tallies to avoid double counting (abstract; Finding 1; Table 6).

Decomposing decisions through the label hierarchy changed results: marginalised reconstruction lowered Jev's accuracy by 11.8-22.9 points (CLINC150 91.0% to 68.1%, [-24.9, -20.9]) and raised the much weaker Laya's by 5.6-21.3, so composed decision chains do not reproduce direct decisions (Table 4, Sec. 7).

Asking the same event through Jev's Event (yes/no) and Choice interfaces gave different act/defer actions on 32.8% of pairs at defer cost 0.10 (post-trained generative readout 34.2%, Kev 14.9%), and inter-interface disagreement certified only 11-52% of error (Abstract, Sec. 6.3, 7, Table 3).

Opinion post: because Jev returns only a floating-point number with no justification, the content signals behind a decision cannot be inspected and hidden bias is hard to detect, so bias should be a primary concern (e.g. ranking job applicants); a single informal 'Good city?' probe is anecdotal (section 'Black boxes are back in fashion').

The note frames the pilot as mechanism evidence only: PASS as a reproducible experiment, ESCALATE for legal conclusions, BLOCK for real files or automated decisions; no auditability of decisions is measured (Estado section).

Normative essay arguing that removing natural-language reasoning traces weakens audit, responsibility attribution and alignment-faking detection, and that calibration is not logical reliability; no data (Sec. 2-4).

On 200 ZebraLogic puzzles, showing GPT-5.6 Luna Jev's probabilities during revision added nothing beyond a Jev-triggered plain second look (43.0% vs 44.5% without reasoning; 97.0% vs 97.0% at high effort) and on flagged items fixed 3 answers but broke 6, so Jev's number worked as a trigger but did not inform the revision (Sec. 6.2, Table 4).

Methods note proposing source-separated, participant-reviewed Choice/Score/Noul question proposals with provenance; only 14/14 synthetic software-contract tests passed and no live Jev call was evaluated (abstract; Sec. 5, 7).

Archived AI-assisted dialogue (ChatGPT, Perplexity responses) arguing that Jev's guarantee is syntactic and that typed inference can relocate ontology-governance commitments into schemas, rubrics, thresholds and compute graphs that are less visible and less contestable; no measurement (full PDF read).

Self-reported fields (truncated, fits, probability, band) were wrong or misleading, e.g. 'probability' is P(selected option) and flips every 'false' answer, but the paper attributes them to access layers (third-party wrapper and plugin), not the engines; provider-returned probabilities and confidence were not shown untrustworthy (Sec. 3.1.1; Results B 3.4-3.8).

excluded_reason: deterministic rule engine; no typed model despite the name
rationale: Per-node rule traceability (threshold, evidence and rule recorded for every verdict, conflicts quarantined to U) is demonstrated for a deterministic rule engine, not for any typed decision model; recorded empirical=no so it is excluded from typed-model tallies (Sec. 2, Sec. 6-7, Sec. 13).
Theory: Lemma 2 shows thresholding typed scores makes a composed pipeline's action discontinuous, so per-hop calibration audits miss chain-level flips; simulations only (Abstract, Sec. 4, 7).

Held-out threshold accepts 0.93 of CLINC at realized risk 0.049 (upper bound 0.066) yet the one-sided bound exceeds 5% for every model; out-of-scope acceptance 0.310 (0.195 with an explicit option); only two cascades gain with CI excluding zero and neither reaches hosted-Jev accuracy (§5.1; §5.3; Tables 9-10).

AURC lower than the generative baseline on classification (0.2020 to 0.1351), multi-label (0.2474 to 0.0126) and counting (1.0000 to 0.3890) and unchanged on regression (0.2272/0.2280), supporting confidence-based deferral in-distribution (Table 2; §5.3).

A separate enough-evidence question reaches AUROC 0.95 vs 0.85 for confidence but is 2-6 points less accurate as an acceptance filter; the not-known option gains +0.051 at 50% post-boundary prevalence but -0.034 at 5%; the out-of-scope option flags 89% of CLINC150 off-topic at 3.5% false alarms but 36% of near-scope Banking77 (Table 1; §4.2-4.3; App. C).

Conceptual: confidence thresholds and exception routing reallocate decision rights, and correlated machine evaluators add little independent evidence (cites nine LLM judges worth about two independent votes) (§6.3; §7.5; §9).

Escalating an uncertainty band calibrated on 400 items per predicate against the gpt-6-luna judge raises Shelob mean F1 to 95.7-97.5% (range 91.5-98.7%) from 63.2-66.3% at a fixed threshold (Table 4; §4.3).

Sealed pre-registered Jev + R1-agreement gate + glm-5.2 cascade is non-inferior to glm-5.2 alone (+0.011 [-0.011, 0.033]; +0.016 [0.003, 0.033]) while settling 34.5-38.0% of windows, but only with the independent agreement gate (without it burst recall 0.78 to 0.52) and it leaks look-alike attacks (§3.5; §4.3).

Preregistered confidence cascades matched or beat the partner LLM at lower cost (Gemini 0.674 vs 0.678 at 56% cost; Gemma 0.638 vs 0.626; Haiku 0.639 vs 0.622 at 27% cost), but the preregistered routing hypothesis (>=0.85 accuracy at confidence >=0.9 with >=15% coverage) failed, clearing only 6 of 14 tasks (Sec. 4.4-4.5).

On the frozen 100-task REFLEX-Sim benchmark, act-when-confident with LLM fallback reached 0.95 vs 0.88 success with 72.7% fewer strong calls (McNemar p=0.039) and all 66 autonomous tasks succeeded; but Kimi failed the non-inferiority bound and on tau2-style tasks REFLEX had 0.850 vs 0.900 (strong-only) and 0.917 for a cheaper Flash self-escalation cascade, differences unresolved (Sec. 5.1, 5.4-5.6, Tables 1, 3-5).

Frozen two-order cascade (Jev then GPT-6) was +0.93 points vs GPT-6 alone at 41% of its fee on 1,610 held-out pairs (JudgeBench -0.74 [-2.22, 0.74]) and matched GPT-6 exactly in a pre-specified live test at 75.5% of its fee; but thresholds had to be chosen on about 100 local labels per workload and routing weakened on style-adversarial pairs (AUROC 0.76 vs 0.84) and reference-free prose (Abstract, Sec. 7.4, 8-9).

Probability thresholds become usable only after task-specific isotonic recalibration on a holdout (Jev ECE 0.1235->0.0077; open NLI 0.1072->0.0063); the authors recommend calibration on the intended data before thresholding (Sec. 5.6; App. G).

The router moves a turn only when Jev's per-option probabilities clear 0.80 and otherwise holds it, which held 42% of routable turns in place while 12.5% of moved turns were still false downgrades; savings depend on this hold rule and on unvalidated author tags (Table 3, Fig. 4, Sec. 8).

On Jev's 12 most confident errors per ordinal panel, 242/252 LLM verdicts (96.0%) repeat the wrong answer vs 50.3% expected under independence, and with cross-fitted thresholds no Jev->LLM cascade beats the best single judge by more than 1.5 points (2.0 with oracle thresholds, n.s.), trailing it on 6 of 9 panels (Sec. 5.3, 6.2; Tables 3-4).

With at most 0.5 questions per conversation the ask-or-decide policy is 14.1 points more accurate than never asking and matches a greedy oracle (AUC 0.799 vs 0.797), and on real ABCD dialogues one exchange adds 8.3 [4.9, 11.7] points where it asks and none where it does not, but the 19% error rate at confidence >= 0.99 means acting when confident still passes confident errors (Sec. 7.1-7.2).

A 0.8 confidence gate let 12.6% [7.5, 20.3] of attack flips through (24.1% for observer opinion) while already routing 18.7% of clean answers to review, the opinion pushed 38.0% of confident answers below the gate (+37.5 pp over re-run), and Noul answers carry no confidence, so the gate catches most flips but not all and floods review (Sec. 4.4).

Under the strictest error limits symmetric policies automate nothing on WAInjectBench and 7.63% on R-Judge; separate thresholds reach 47.03% mainly through blocks (110 blocks, 1 allow), passing confirmation does not ensure limits hold on test, and LLM judges catch at most 5 of Jev's 130 high-confidence misses (Sec. 5.3-5.4).

Validation-tuned CPU->NPU confidence cascade achieves 99.23% accuracy, 0.00% FPR and 41.63 ms mean latency, but only on a 130-query live slice and with gating thresholds and fine-tuning fitted to the authors' own domain (Sec. IV-D; Table III).

Jev's gate acted wrongly on at most 0.143 of changed questions (preregistered outcome 6 safe / 1 within bound / 0 violating) vs 0.801 for fine-tuned Laya, but certifying action on any new decision type at alpha=0.05 requires >=19 labels, Jev is 11-29x slower than local models, and labels are simulator-derived (Abstract, Sec. VI-C, IX).

The frozen confidence gate beat random escalation at matched rate (Delta +0.0646 [0.0502, 0.0785], H3b supported) but missed its 10% accepted-set error target out of sample on both tracks (0.140 and 0.103, H3a failed), accepted confidence-1.0 security errors, and case-level gating fell to 5.5% coverage (Sec. 7, Sec. 8.1).

Selective prediction was worse than GPT-6 Sol on two of three benchmarks (AURC 0.087 vs 0.070 on MetaMedQA, 0.303 vs 0.080 on DiagnosisArena; 0.109 vs 0.126 on PubMedQA): 93.4% accuracy at confidence >=0.9 but GPT-6 Sol as accurate at matched coverage, and the authors conclude better calibration gave no selective-prediction advantage (Abstract, Sec. 3.3).

A threshold tau=0.03 on p(None) selected on 20 development problems raises held-out arithmetic rejection from 7% to 79% with present accuracy 99% to 97% (purchase 24 to 79 / 94 to 86); T/F scores keep AUC 0.985 (§5.1; §5.3; Table 2).

As an escalation trigger Jev flagged 93% of Luna's no-reasoning errors at 92% precision but only 70% at 8.5% precision once Luna used high-effort reasoning, and Jev-triggered second looks added 3.5 and 2.0 points; replacing Luna's answer on disagreement changed one correct high-effort answer to wrong (Sec. 6.1-6.3, Tables 4-5).
Design requires human review and participant final decision before any execution, but the note states that oversight effects, harms and Jev outputs were not measured (Sec. 4.5, 7).

Escalating Jev's uncertain band to an LLM rarely helped (2 of 30 cascades significant, both via Sonnet 4.6) because LLM accuracy inside the band was 0.21-0.85, so the author recommends routing that band to a human; Jev's own risk-coverage curves were monotone (98.6% accuracy at 80% coverage on ToxicChat) (Sec. 4-5, Tables 10-11).

Technical note proposing a Decision Orchestration Layer in which a decision below a validated confidence threshold escalates to a more capable model and high-risk decisions go to a human, stressing that thresholds must be measured on labelled workflow data; no measurement (Sec. 12, Sec. 17).

On a prespecified 204-item holdout a Laya >=0.90 gate avoided 60.8% of phi4:14b calls with cascade accuracy 181/204 vs 180/204 for phi4 (+0.5 pp, 95% CI -2.5 to +3.9), meeting all criteria, but the threshold was chosen on a pilot and all 8 accepted errors bypassed escalation (Sec. 3.2-3.3).

A fixed probability gate removed Jev's 6 false allows but withheld 29 additional correct allows (298 vs 327 of 345), a development-selected gate kept zero false allows at 320/345, the gate left GPT-4.1 mini's 13 false allows unchanged, and DeepSeek reached zero false allows with more correct allows (315 vs 295) (Table III, Sec. V-D, V-E).

A coverage-matched threshold sent every attacked wrong answer to review (0/90, upper bound 3.3%) and a fixed 0.8 gate passed none as served, but at raw T=1 three attacked errors passed 0.8; protection was a side effect of confidence dropping and attacks forced reviews and false blocks (36/46 safe commands flipped) (Sec. 5.2, 5.5, 6.1).

On 300 authored allow/hold/deny cases (one session per model), Jev's 28 errors concentrated on hold references (9 allowed and 16 denied of 111), 10 of them at selected probability >= 0.9 (our count from the workbook), KEV-4B erred similarly and the open CLM v0.1-8B held all 300 cases, while Jev's correctness AUROC (0.82) exceeded the self-reported GLM 5.3 FlashX (0.73) (RESULTS-SUMMARY; workbook Results sheet).

With a confidence threshold fixed on calibration data, basal-1.0-4.5B auto-decided 58.6% of test decisions at 1.2% observed error (target 1%) vs 18.1% coverage for Jev under the same procedure, after per-decision-type calibration and on author-generated items whose test split was consulted during development (Abstract, Contributions, Limitations).

A coverage-matched gate (tau50) let none of 589 attack flips through, but a fixed 0.8 gate on raw scores passed 42, and notes agreeing with existing mistakes produced 14 oversight switch-offs per temperature that cleared both decision and review gates; a second call without the untrusted text caught all flips but none of these boosted mistakes (Sec. 5.3-5.5).

A conformal escalation gate built on Laya's confidence returned risk 0.585 at nominal alpha=0.05; a frozen-encoder refit-head control attributes about 70% of the failure to representation (Abstract, Sec. 4.2).

Read 6,840 screen hits under an 8-question schema plus 499,306 random narratives of a 5.0M statewide corpus (adjusted total 5,467 [5,306, 5,577]) but only with a regex pre-screen, blind stratified human audit and Rogan-Gladen correction; cost not reported and identifiers remained in 37-43% of redacted narratives (§1; §3.1; Table 7).

Hosted Jev costs US$0.0079 per 1,000 decisions at median 138 ms (p95 183) vs Qwen3-14B verbal US$0.0265 and 995 ms; some open typed checkpoints are cheaper still (this-that-model-1.0 US$0.0020) (Table 8).

52,000 Jev-40 decisions cost US$14.68 at median latency 0.750 s vs 6.036 s for Sol (US$0.028 vs US$5.61 per 100 paired responses), but accuracy far below small trained trees removes the practical benefit (Tables 2-3; §4.5).

Hosted jev-1.13.0 scoring took 1.4-2.1x as long as local Qwen finite scoring on all eight tasks (variant end-to-end 43.96-249.05 s) with mixed quality (Sokoban 0.250 vs 0.150; RushHour 0.290 vs 0.390); cost not reported (§4.2; Tables 1-2).
Mean latency 0.31-0.34 s vs 1.99-2.65 s and US$43-295 vs US$1,068-3,035 per million flow decisions for Gemini 3.6 Flash (7.7x faster and 22x cheaper at k=1) (Table 4; §6.4).

Conceptual: a conditional Jevons hypothesis that cheaper machine evaluation may raise total evaluation and exception-handling demand; the relevant cost is a usable evaluative act within a workflow (§5).

JEVDB-Flash is fastest on all 21 SemBench queries and cheapest on 19 (41.50 s and US$1.06 total vs LOTUS 3,709 s/US$14.28 and Palimpzest 2,988 s/US$19.81), and full JEVDB finishes Shelob tier M where no baseline finishes within 1,200 s (Table 3; §4.2-4.3).
Median Jev compute 1.22 s (10th-90th 1.15-1.46) over 2,722 calls vs 30.6-31.7 s for glm-5.2 and 39.3-46.4 s for deepseek-v4-pro per decision; monetary cost not reported (§3.4).

Coded 195,857 Texas crash narratives at about $0.154 per 1,000 vs $7.95 for a mid-tier LLM (52x), with F1 0.908 vs 0.967 and 0.885 for two frontier models against human labels; probabilities usable for ranking but prevalence counts need per-variable recalibration and a review budget over flagged records (Sec. 4.1, 4.3-4.4, 5).

KITE runs 1M agents x 20 steps in 0.9 s and passes content-fidelity gates in all 15 new countries, but intervention effects need sparse flagship-LLM anchors (Epstein effect MAE 0.0305->0.0180) and the preregistered primary policy-value gain was not shown (hybrid minus kernel 0.0027 [-0.0118, 0.0169]) (abstract; Sec. 5; Table D1).

In an emulated 10,000-seat enterprise built from 46 synthetic scenarios (109 turns) and public session corpora, Jev-labelled cache-safe routing recovered 13.4% of model spend ($3.3M/yr) vs 20.8% with perfect labels, with per-axis classifier accuracy 63-82% and author-only ground-truth tags; Jev is not self-hostable, so a self-hosted encoder is the stated fallback (Table 3, Sec. 4.6, Sec. 5.1, Sec. 8).

Repository mining of 2,170 public Jev projects (1,865 created in the first week) shows broad adoption across 8 domains, but Safety & Governance is 175 projects (8.1%) with about 3.5% of stars while routing/automation holds 41.4% of stars; labels assigned by LLM agents (Table 1; Sec. 2).

SubJudge matches or surpasses frontier LLMs on several personalised-judgement metrics (PluriHarms aggregated MAE 0.2278 vs 0.228 GPT-5.4; iNews arousal MAE 0.7530 vs 0.8929) with 1.29-261x lower latency than Qwen3.5-9B, but not on every metric (e.g. iNews valence) (abstract; Sec. 3.1; Table 2).

For evaluating public-policy arguments Jev showed small source effects but compressed, unexplained scores (no written assessment), which the author says reduces the visibility of any bias and limits comparison with chat evaluators; the study does not test deployment at scale (Sec. 4.4, 5, App. B).

Used as a stand-in for survey respondents, Jev defaults to an American value profile, captures only 62% of the human Saudi-US difference in Arabic, and mis-ranks 33% of dimensions with no matched profile having all six in order, so simulated publics lean to one culture (Sec. 4.8, Sec. 5.3).

Median per-user latency 350-967 ms up to K=200 vs Qwen2.5-7B pointwise 6.07-14.87 s, but SASRec/DCNv2 under 1.3 ms, latency not hardware-normalized and no cost reported; ranking best in most cells but SASRec higher HR@10 on Movies K=200 (0.170 vs 0.150) (Tables 2-3; §6.3).

On the author's 10 civic triage scenarios Jev reached 100% routing accuracy and schema compliance at 197.6 ms mean and $0.05 per 100,000 queries, while generative LLMs took 3,340-12,682 ms in emergency scenarios and Qwen reached 33.3% standalone accuracy; very small self-built scenario set (Public-service paper Abstract, Table 1, Sec. 5.1-5.2).

410 requests cost $0.0081 at a median 275 ms whether or not the model was undecided (274 vs 272 ms; humans 4.6-6.8 s), so the difficulty-correlated latency institutions use to flag hard cases disappears; agreement with the film's decisions was partial (11 of 29) (paper Abstract, Sec. IV-A, V).

Because Jev stays confident on items where 100 annotators split (40% of hard items at confidence >= 0.9 with mean agreement 0.505), its probabilities do not estimate how many people would agree, which limits its use as a stand-in for population judgement (Abstract, Sec. 8).

Jev was the fastest and cheapest model, but its political defaults in structured outputs depended on instrument, script and stated asker (with a Beijing asker it chose PRC formulations on all three sovereignty questions in Simplified Chinese and English, as did both Claude models); the label-side swap was specific to Claude Sonnet 5 per the addendum (Abstract, Sec. 4.7, 4.9, App. C).
